name: Topological Approach
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Betting on Physics Instead of Engineering
lesson.summary: Topological qubits try to make fragility a nonissue by hiding information in the shape of a system rather than a physical spot, a strategy still unproven after decades of effort.
lesson.body:
Every platform covered so far treats fragility as an engineering problem to be minimized: cool the chip colder, isolate the atom better, lose fewer photons. The topological approach takes a fundamentally different bet. Instead of trying to protect a fragile qubit from noise after the fact, it tries to build a qubit that is intrinsically hard to disturb, because the information is not stored in any single, local physical spot that noise can reach.

The idea rests on exotic quasiparticles called non-abelian anyons, and in particular a proposed excitation called a Majorana zero mode, predicted to appear at the ends of certain semiconductor nanowires coupled to superconductors. The claim is that if a qubit's state is encoded in the joint, nonlocal configuration of a pair of these modes, rather than in one particle's local properties, then small local disturbances, a stray photon, a tiny electric field fluctuation, cannot easily flip the encoded information, because there is no single local place to flip. Operations would be performed by physically braiding these quasiparticles around each other, with the topology of the braid itself, not fine tuned pulse timing, determining the result. In principle this offers a kind of built in error protection that other platforms have to bolt on afterward through active error correction.

The trouble is that this protection has been extraordinarily hard to demonstrate convincingly. For years, groups reported signatures consistent with Majorana zero modes, only for later, more careful analysis to show the evidence was ambiguous. A widely discussed 2018 result from a Delft University group, published with support from Microsoft, claimed to observe quantized conductance consistent with Majorana modes, and was retracted in 2021 after independent reanalysis found the original data presentation had selectively excluded contradicting measurements. That retraction was a serious blow to confidence in the field's ability to distinguish a genuine topological signature from ordinary disorder effects that can mimic it.

Microsoft has continued pursuing this approach, announcing a chip built around this architecture in early 2025 and describing it as a step toward a topological qubit. The announcement drew immediate and pointed skepticism from parts of the physics community, with several researchers arguing that the published evidence did not yet establish the topological protection the architecture depends on, only some of the precursor ingredients. This is not unusual for the field: topological approaches have repeatedly produced results that looked promising in isolation and proved difficult to fully verify.

What makes this approach worth including here, despite its unresolved status, is what it represents: an attempt to solve the qubits are extremely fragile problem at the level of physics itself rather than through better refrigeration or faster lasers. If it works, it could sidestep much of the overhead burdening every other platform. Whether the underlying physics actually delivers that protection in a controllable, scalable device is, as of this writing, still an open and genuinely contested question, not a solved engineering problem waiting for better manufacturing.
